Method of Attack: Emotet is spread through phishing emails with malicious Word document attachments pretending to be invoices, shipping notices, account reports, holiday party invites, or Coronavirus information.
Once installed, Emotet uses the infected computer to send spam and download other malware.
Emotet commonly downloads and installs the Trickbot banking Trojan, which steals saved credentials, cookies, browser history, SSH keys, and attempts to spread on the network.
Trickbot opens a reverse shell to Ryuk ransomware operators who encrypt the network as a final payload.
Attack Vector: Phishing emails with malicious Word document attachments
Indicators of Compromise: Emotet installed under semi-random folder in %LocalAppData% named by combining two keywords from a specific list (e.g., 'symbolguid').
Process detected by EmoCheck utility (emocheck_x64.exe or emocheck_x86.exe).
Log files named yyyymmddhhmmss_emocheck.txt generated by EmoCheck.
